dublinCore.title: A Convolutional Layer Is a Learned FIR Filter
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Convolutional neural networks
FIR filters
Frequency response
Machine learning in DSP
Gradient descent
Signal classification
dublinCore.description: Trains a tiny 1-D convolutional network (F kernels of K taps, ReLU, global max-pool, logistic output) in the browser with hand-written gradient descent to tell a low tone (0.08 cycles/sample) from a high tone (0.30 cycles/sample) in noise. Stem plots of the learned kernels and their frequency responses show that the kernels become band-pass FIR filters tuned to the tones, alongside loss and accuracy curves and four test segments with predictions.
relation: Chapter 15: Signal Processing Applications and AI Integration

searchKeywords: what does a CNN learn on signals

learningObjectives: Explain how a convolutional layer computes z_f[n] as an FIR filter (written as a cross-correlation), followed by ReLU and global max-pooling
Analyze a trained kernel's frequency response to decide which tone it detects, using the peak of |H(f)|, the ratio |H(0.30)|/|H(0.08)| and the sign of its output weight v
Relate the kernel length K to frequency resolution and predict when a kernel can form a peak at the low tone
Evaluate how the learning rate and the noise level affect convergence, stability and test accuracy
Design a hand-made kernel that detects the high tone and compare its frequency response with the learned kernel's
prerequisites: Frequency response of an FIR filter
Classifiers trained by gradient descent on a loss function

misconceptions.misconception: The weights of a neural network cannot be interpreted
misconceptions.correction: Each trained kernel is an FIR filter whose frequency response can be read like any other filter's
misconceptions.evidence: After pressing Run with the default settings the kernels peak at 0.304 and 0.081 cycles/sample, within 0.004 of the tones they vote for, and the sign of the output weight tells which tone

misconceptions.misconception: A CNN convolution is the same as the convolution of Chapter 4
misconceptions.correction: A CNN layer computes a cross-correlation with no kernel flip; flipping changes only the phase of H(f), so |H(f)| and the band-pass interpretation are unchanged
misconceptions.evidence: The sim computes z_f[n] = sum_k w_f[k] x[n + k] and plots |H(f)| = |sum_k w[k] e^{-j 2 pi f k}|

misconceptions.misconception: A larger learning rate always trains faster
misconceptions.correction: Too large a step can flip a kernel's role or make the weights diverge
misconceptions.evidence: eta = 1 turns the low-tone kernel into a second high-tone kernel and ends at 88.3% test accuracy instead of 96.5%; eta = 3 diverges at step 11

accessibility.screenReaderScript: A tiny one-dimensional convolutional network learns to tell a low tone at 0.08 cycles per sample from a high tone at 0.30 cycles per sample in noise. Stem plots show each learned kernel, a second plot shows each kernel frequency response with gold markers at the two tone frequencies, two plots show the loss and accuracy during training, and four test segments are drawn with the predicted class. Buttons run, step, reset and draw new data; sliders set the noise level, learning rate, kernel size and number of filters.

controls.label: Run / Pause
controls.description: Starts or pauses training; a run stops at step 400, and Run then starts again from step 0

controls.label: Step
controls.description: Pauses and applies one gradient-descent step on a batch of 16 training segments

controls.label: Reset
controls.description: Restores the seeded starting weights, clears the curves and waits at step 0

controls.label: New data
controls.description: Draws a new seeded training set and test set and restarts training

controls.label: Noise sigma
controls.description: Standard deviation of the white Gaussian noise added to every segment (the tones have amplitude 1)

controls.label: Learning rate eta
controls.description: Selects the gradient-descent learning rate from 0.001, 0.003, 0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1 and 3

controls.label: Kernel size K
controls.description: Number of taps in each convolution kernel

controls.label: Filters F
controls.description: Number of convolution kernels (filters) in the layer

visualElements.description: Stem plots of the learned kernel taps w_f[k], one per filter
Frequency response |H(f)| of each kernel from 0 to 0.5 cycles/sample with gold markers at 0.08 and 0.30 and a dot at each peak
Table of each kernel's peak frequency, gain ratio |H(0.30)|/|H(0.08)| in dB and output weight v
Training and test cross-entropy loss and accuracy versus training step
Four test segments (blue) over their clean tone (gold) with p(high), the predicted class, and bars marking each kernel's max-pool winner

model.description: Binary classification of 64-sample segments sin(2 pi f n + phase) + sigma w[n] with f = 0.08 (class 0) or 0.30 (class 1). A 1-D convolutional layer with F kernels of K taps, ReLU, global max-pooling and a logistic output is trained by plain mini-batch gradient descent (batch 16) on 256 training segments for up to 400 steps and evaluated on 256 test segments. All data and initial weights are seeded.
equations: z_f[n] = sum_k w_f[k] x[n + k] + b_f, n = 0 .. 64 - K
L = -[y ln p + (1 - y) ln(1 - p)]
dL/dw_f[k] = (p - y) v_f x[n* + k] when a_f > 0
algorithms: Mini-batch gradient descent with hand-written backpropagation
Seeded mulberry32 random numbers with Box-Muller Gaussian noise
limitations: Plain gradient descent with no momentum, weight decay or learning-rate schedule
The output weights start at +0.5, -0.5, +0.5, which sets each kernel's initial role

instructionalStrategies: Step through the first few gradient updates and watch the kernel's frequency response form
Predict-then-verify with the kernel size and learning-rate sliders
Compare a learned kernel with a hand-designed windowed sinusoid
extensions: Add a third tone class and a softmax output
Replace global max-pooling with average pooling and compare the learned kernels
